overview.title: Why scale training, and the two kinds of parallelism
overview.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world
overview.section: 18.2 Scaling up model training with multiple devices
overview.main_topic: Training speed as the bottleneck of the loop of progress; data parallelism versus model parallelism
overview.central_idea: Once you can write experiments quickly, the speed of training becomes the limit on how fast you improve. Using several devices removes that limit, either by giving each device a copy of the model and its own slice of the data (data parallelism), or by splitting one model across devices (model parallelism).
overview.importance: This page frames the whole of section 18.2. The two terms it defines, data parallelism and model parallelism, are used on every following page through the DeviceMesh and LayoutMap APIs (p.576-578).
learning_objectives: Explain why training speed limits the quality of deep learning work, using the loop of progress (figure 18.1).
Define data parallelism and model parallelism and say what is replicated or split in each.
State when model parallelism is used in practice (models too large for one device) and why it is not mainly a speed-up tool.
Describe how the two forms of parallelism can be combined (e.g., 4 devices per model copy x 2 copies = 8 devices).
prerequisites: The loop of progress and TensorBoard from chapter 7 (p.236)
Mini-batch training and the batch axis (p.49-50)
Model ensembling, which this page finishes (p.570-571)

summary:
The page opens with the last sentences of the ensembling discussion: one model in the authors' Kaggle example helped the ensemble because it was **different** from all the others and gave information they lacked. The point of ensembling is the diversity of the candidate models, not the strength of the best one.

Section **18.2** then starts. It goes back to the *loop of progress* from chapter 7 (figure 18.1): an **idea** becomes an **experiment** (with a framework such as Keras), the experiment runs on **GPUs/TPUs** and produces **results**, and the results are analysed (for example with TensorBoard) to give the next idea. How good your ideas get depends on how many turns of this loop you can make. Once you are fluent with Keras, writing the experiment stops being the slow step and **training time** becomes the bottleneck. If a run takes 10-15 minutes, you can do dozens of iterations a day, so faster training directly gives better models.

Section **18.2.1** starts from the observation that models are growing faster than single GPUs, so one GPU puts a hard limit on progress. The answer is *multi-GPU distributed training*, and there are two ways to do it:

- **Data parallelism**: the whole model is copied to each device (or machine). Each copy processes different batches of data, and the results are merged.
- **Model parallelism**: different parts of one model run on different devices and work together on the same batch. It suits architectures that are naturally parallel, such as multi-branch models. In practice it is used **only when a model is too large for any single device**. It is a way to train bigger models, not a way to speed up ordinary ones.

Finally, the two can be **mixed**: a model is split across, say, 4 devices, and that split model is then replicated (the sentence continues on p.573 with 2 x 4 = 8 devices).

paragraphs.excerpt: was so different from every other model: it provided information that the other models
paragraphs.what_it_says: This finishes the ensembling story from p.571. The model that helped the ensemble most was valuable because it was unlike the others and contributed information they did not have. The authors conclude that ensembling depends on the diversity of the candidate set, not on the quality of the single best model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Averaging models only helps when their errors differ. If all models make the same mistakes, averaging them repeats those mistakes. A weaker model that is wrong in *different* places can still lower the ensemble's error.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It closes section 18.1. In practice, add models built on different principles (for example a tree-based model and a deep net) instead of many near-copies of one architecture.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: for an average of M predictors with error variance sigma^2 and pairwise error correlation rho, the ensemble variance is rho*sigma^2 + (1-rho)*sigma^2/M. Diversity (low rho) is what makes the second term shrink.

terminology.meaning: Pooling the predictions of several models (for example by a weighted average) to get better predictions than any one of them.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors recall the loop of progress from chapter 7. The quality of an idea depends on how many refinement cycles it has gone through. The speed of each cycle depends on three things: how fast you set up an experiment, how fast it runs, and how well you analyse the results.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Progress in deep learning is empirical and iterative, so the number of loops per day matters a great deal. Each of the three stages can be the slow one. Figure 18.1 labels the tools for each stage: Keras for idea to experiment, GPUs/TPUs for experiment to results, and TensorBoard for results to the next idea.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why a book about deep learning spends a section on hardware scaling: the goal is faster iteration, not big compute for its own sake.

terminology.meaning: The cycle idea -> experiment -> results -> new idea that drives empirical model development (figure 7.6 / 18.1).

connections: p.236: the loop of progress was introduced alongside TensorBoard (figure 7.6)

paragraphs.what_it_says: As you get better at Keras, coding experiments stops being the bottleneck and training speed becomes the next one. With fast infrastructure you get results in 10-15 minutes and can do dozens of iterations a day. Faster training directly improves the quality of your solutions. The section will show how to use multiple GPUs or TPUs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a bottleneck argument: speed up the slowest stage of the loop. A 10-minute turnaround allows about 40-50 experiments in a working day. An 8-hour turnaround allows one. That is a different way of working.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It motivates everything in 18.2 and 18.3. Distributed training (this section) and mixed precision (p.583) are both ways to shorten the experiment-to-results arrow.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the claim treats iteration count as the main driver of model quality. The same idea underlies hyperparameter search (p.563), where faster trials mean more of the search space can be covered.

p.583: mixed-precision training is another way to speed up the experiment stage

paragraphs.what_it_says: GPUs get more powerful every year, but models grow even faster and need more compute. A single GPU puts a hard limit on how fast you can move. The solution is to add more GPUs and do multi-GPU distributed training.
paragraphs.what_it_means: One device has a fixed amount of compute (FLOP/s) and memory. Past that limit, the only option is to use several devices together, which brings the coordination problems discussed next.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It introduces the term *multi-GPU distributed training*, which the rest of the section makes concrete.

terminology.meaning: Training one model using several devices (GPUs/TPUs), possibly across several machines, that cooperate on each training step.

connections: p.579: TPU training extends the same ideas to TPU pods

paragraphs.excerpt: There are two ways to distribute computation across multiple devices: data parallelism and model
paragraphs.what_it_says: There are two ways to spread computation across devices: data parallelism and model parallelism.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The question is which thing you split: the data (each device gets different samples) or the model (each device gets different parameters and the computation that uses them).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Every distribution strategy that follows, including the DeviceMesh axes named "data" and "model" on p.576, comes from this split.

terminology.meaning: Replicating the model and splitting the data across devices.
Splitting the model across devices that work on the same data.

connections: p.576: a DeviceMesh has one axis per form of parallelism

paragraphs.excerpt: With data parallelism, a single model gets replicated on multiple devices or multiple machines.
paragraphs.what_it_says: In data parallelism, one model is replicated on several devices or machines. Each replica processes different batches of data, and the results are then merged.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each device holds the full set of weights. The merge step differs by mode: predictions are concatenated at inference time, and gradients are averaged during training (spelled out on p.573).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the simplest and most common way to speed up training, and in Keras it takes one line (p.575).

terminology.meaning: A full copy of the model living on one device.

connections: p.573: details of inference vs. training under data parallelism

paragraphs.excerpt: With model parallelism, different parts of a single model run on different devices, processing
paragraphs.what_it_says: In model parallelism, different parts of one model run on different devices and process the same batch together. It works best for naturally parallel architectures such as multi-branch models. In practice it is used only for models too large to fit on any single device. It is a way to train larger models, not to speed up regular ones.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Splitting a model means devices must exchange activations during every forward and backward pass, which costs communication. That cost is worth paying only when you cannot fit the model on one device at all. A multi-branch model (functional API, p.217-219) splits naturally because each branch can run on its own device.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It corrects a common intuition. Model parallelism is mainly about **memory capacity**, not throughput. For a model that fits on one device, data parallelism is almost always faster.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: modern model parallelism is usually 'tensor parallelism' (splitting the matrices inside each layer). The book calls this vertical partitioning (p.574). Splitting by layer is 'pipeline parallelism' (horizontal partitioning).

terminology.meaning: A model whose graph has parallel paths (e.g., Inception-style), naturally separable across devices.

connections: p.219: multi-input/multi-branch models built with the functional API

paragraphs.what_it_says: The two can be combined: a model can be split across several devices (e.g., 4), and that split model can then be replicated. The sentence continues on p.573.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Model parallelism handles memory (each group of 4 devices together holds one model). Data parallelism handles throughput (several such groups each process a different sub-batch).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This hybrid is how very large models are actually trained, and it is the setup the Keras example on p.576-578 builds: a 2 x 4 mesh.

concepts.name: Loop of progress
concepts.definition: The iterative cycle idea -> experiment -> results -> next idea (figure 18.1).
concepts.intuition: The more turns you can make in a day, the faster your ideas improve.
concepts.technical: Figure 18.1 maps each arrow to a tool: Keras (idea to experiment), GPUs/TPUs (experiment to results), TensorBoard (results to idea). Whichever arrow is slowest bounds the iteration rate.
concepts.significance: It is the reason for investing in faster training.
concepts.example: 10-15 minute training runs allow dozens of iterations per day (book).
concepts.misconception: That the loop is only about hardware. The book says setting up and analysing the experiment matter as much as running it.

concepts.name: Data parallelism
concepts.definition: Replicating the full model on each device and having each replica process a different part of the data.
concepts.intuition: Many identical workers, each grading a different stack of exams, then pooling notes.
concepts.technical: Each replica computes gradients on its own sub-batch. The gradients are averaged across replicas (an all-reduce), and every replica applies the same update.
concepts.significance: The default and most scalable way to speed up training of models that fit on one device.
concepts.example: Two GPUs, a batch of 128 split into two sub-batches of 64 (p.573).
concepts.misconception: That it lets you train models larger than one device's memory. It does not, because each device holds the whole model.

concepts.name: Model parallelism
concepts.definition: Splitting one model's parameters and computation across several devices that cooperate on the same batch.
concepts.intuition: One very large document split among several typists, each writing different pages of the same copy.
concepts.technical: Requires exchanging activations between devices within each step; used when parameters plus optimizer state exceed one device's memory.
concepts.significance: Makes models with tens of billions of parameters trainable.
concepts.example: Listing 18.4's 1.5-billion-parameter dense model split across two small devices (p.573-574).
concepts.misconception: That it is a general speed-up technique. The book says it is not used to speed up regular models.

concepts.name: Multi-GPU distributed training
concepts.definition: Training one model with several accelerators working together on each step.
concepts.intuition: Adding workers to a job, with some coordination overhead.
concepts.technical: Implemented in Keras 3 via keras.distribution (DataParallel, DeviceMesh, LayoutMap, ModelParallel), best supported on the JAX backend (p.574-575).
concepts.significance: Removes the single-device ceiling on speed and model size.
concepts.example: Eight GPUs organised as two replicas of four devices (figure 18.2).
concepts.misconception: That N GPUs give exactly N times the speed. See the measured speedups on p.576.

deeper.title: Why model parallelism is not a speed-up tool for ordinary models
deeper.body: Beyond the book. Suppose a model fits on one GPU. With **data parallelism** on 2 GPUs, each GPU does half the samples, and the only communication is one gradient all-reduce per step (about the size of the parameters). With **model parallelism** on 2 GPUs, each GPU does half of every layer's math, but the devices must exchange activations at layer boundaries in **both** the forward and backward pass. Activations scale with batch size times layer width, and this exchange sits on the critical path of every layer. Each device also gets smaller matrix multiplications, which use the hardware less efficiently. So for a model that fits, data parallelism nearly always wins. Model parallelism is worth its cost only when the alternative is not being able to train the model.

deeper.title: Iteration speed as a multiplier
deeper.body: Illustration (not from the book): a working day of 8 hours with a 15-minute run allows about 32 sequential experiments. With an 8-hour run you get 1. Going from 1 GPU to 8 GPUs at the 7.3x speedup quoted on p.576 turns a 2-hour run into about 16 minutes, which takes you from about 4 iterations a day to about 30.

misconceptions.claim: Model parallelism is a general way to make training faster.
misconceptions.correction: The book says model parallelism is used only for models too large for a single device. It is a way to train larger models, not to speed up regular ones.

misconceptions.claim: The best ensemble is built from the strongest individual models.
misconceptions.correction: The book stresses diversity: a model that is different and brings new information can help more than another strong but similar model.

misconceptions.claim: Compute speed only matters for production.
misconceptions.correction: Training speed sets how many refinement cycles you get, so it directly affects the quality of research and development.

takeaways: Ensembling works because of diversity among models, not the strength of the best model.
Once coding is fast, training speed becomes the bottleneck of the loop of progress, and faster training means better models.
Data parallelism replicates the whole model and splits the data. Model parallelism splits the model and shares the data.
Model parallelism is used for models that do not fit on one device, not to speed up regular models.
The two can be combined: split a model over a group of devices, then replicate that group.

questions.question: According to the book, when is model parallelism used in practice?
options: Whenever you have more than one GPU
Only when the model is too large to fit on any single device
questions.answer: Only when the model is too large to fit on any single device
questions.explanation: The page says model parallelism is used only for models too large for one device, as a way to train larger models. Having several GPUs alone calls for data parallelism. Inference and batch size are not the criteria.

questions.question: In data parallelism, what is replicated and what is split?
questions.answer: The model is replicated on every device. The data (each batch) is split so that each replica processes different samples.
questions.explanation: This is the definition in e10, expanded on p.573.

questions.question: Why does the book argue that faster training directly improves the quality of deep learning solutions?
questions.answer: Model quality comes from many refinement cycles of the loop of progress. Once writing experiments is fast, training time limits how many cycles you can do, so shorter runs (10-15 minutes) allow dozens of iterations a day and more refinement.
questions.explanation: This follows the e05/e07 reasoning around figure 18.1.

questions.question: Which tool does figure 18.1 attach to the 'Results -> Idea' arrow?
questions.explanation: Figure 18.1 labels Idea->Experiment with Keras, Experiment->Results with GPUs/TPUs, and Results->Idea with the visualization framework TensorBoard. KerasTuner is not in the figure.

questions.question: Which kind of architecture does the book say suits model parallelism best, and why?
questions.answer: Models with a naturally parallel architecture, such as multi-branch models, because separate branches can run on separate devices at the same time with little dependence on each other.
questions.explanation: Stated in e10. The 'why' is the natural reading: independent branches need little communication between devices.

questions.question: If a model is split across 4 devices and that split model is replicated twice, how many devices are used, and which form of parallelism does each factor correspond to?
questions.answer: 8 devices. The factor 4 is model parallelism (split within a replica) and the factor 2 is data parallelism (number of replicas).
questions.explanation: Last sentence of the page, completed on p.573 (2 * 4 = 8).

questions.question: Think of your last project: which arrow of the loop of progress was your real bottleneck? Would multiple GPUs have helped?
questions.answer: Open answer. If runs took hours, multi-GPU data parallelism would help. If analysis or setup was slow, better tooling (Keras, TensorBoard) matters more.
questions.explanation: The book's point is to find and attack the slowest stage of the loop.
